name: RampMeter
one_liner: A day-ahead traffic report for PacifiCorp East, built on free CAISO and EIA data. It tells every Torus Station how much power to keep open for Rocky Mountain Power's surprise calls, then spends the rest of the battery on the host's demand-charge peak and the grid's evening rush hour.
options_covered:
Option 1 is the core and gets about 85% of the effort. It has two halves. The "traffic report for tomorrow's grid" is built from real EDAM day-ahead prices (including the congestion component), CAISO load and wind/solar forecasts, and EIA-930 fuel mix and CO2. "Staying out of traffic" is a reservation planner for a simulated fleet of Torus-style stations.

Option 2 comes in only through its "when" half, as one more host type in the same planner: an AI training cluster. In red hours its deferrable jobs move or its GPUs are power-capped. The cap is priced on Emerald AI's public power-cap sweep, where capping A100s at 300 W keeps 86-95% of throughput (prior-art.findings.md). Pulse is then free to serve the grid.

The "where" half (a router across regions) is deliberately left out of the core, for three reasons:
- Torus does not route compute between regions (torus-intel.findings.md).
- Torus's data-center pages went 404 between 2026-08-04 and 2026-10-26 (torus-intel.findings.md).
- Carbon-aware job routers are the most crowded hackathon pattern: at least 9 near-identical entries, and EuroSys 2024 found their savings modest (prior-art.findings.md).

If we finish early, a one-panel "where" cameo can reuse prices already in the snapshot. Tomorrow at 10am SP15 is $9.14/MWh against $23.23 in PACE (pace_snapshot_2026-10-27.csv). It is first on the cut list.
the_insight:
Rocky Mountain Power's call on a Torus Station is a promise of power (kW), not of stored energy (kWh). Keeping that promise costs about six minutes of full power. The rest of each station is free to work the hours that can be predicted a day ahead.

The numbers behind it:

1) The calls are random in time and small in energy.
- Torus reports 359 unplanned events in 2025, mostly fast frequency response. Each holds about 5-6 minutes after a 19-second ramp, and RMP dispatches in less than 1% of hours (torus-cases-a.findings.md).
- Derived: 359 x 5.5 min is about 33 hours a year, or 0.38% of hours.
- Torus's own hour-of-day chart has events in every hour. The busiest hour holds only 41 of the 359 (11%). The chart states no time zone, so nothing here depends on when the calls land. That is the point: they cannot be scheduled, only covered.

2) The hardware already fits that promise.
- Derived from Torus's 0.5C Pulse spec: a full-power 5.5-minute call drains about 4.6% of a Pulse.
- Torus Spin discharges fully in 6 minutes at 10C, so one Spin sized to the enrolled kW is roughly one call (torus-cases-b.findings.md).
- So the RMP lane is mostly Spin plus spare Pulse power. It is not a battery held at high charge.

3) The grid's rush hour, unlike the calls, is published the night before.
- For Oct 27, PACE's day-ahead price is $21.38 at 3pm and $55.78 at 6pm (2.6x), while EDAM solar falls from 2,056 MW at 4pm to 36 MW at 6pm (pace_snapshot_2026-10-27.csv).
- Across Oct 1-25, 6-7pm averaged $57.0 against $28.6 at 11am. The priciest 10% of October hours ran 85.1% fossil, the cheapest 10% ran 39.8% (utah-grid.findings.md).
- EIA's hourly PACE CO2 on Oct 25 ranged from 504 g/kWh to 817 (data-option1.findings.md).

4) The scarce resource is Pulse's cycle life, not its charge.
- Torus publishes 7,500 Pulse cycles, 25,000 Spin cycles and a 25-year life. Spread evenly (derived, and assuming Pulse is not repowered), that is about 300 Pulse cycles a year against about 1,000 for Spin.
- RMP's 359 calls would use about 36% of Spin's yearly budget but only about 16 Pulse equivalent cycles.
- So the planner spends Pulse cycles only on days whose spread pays. The median daily day-ahead spread was $27.2/MWh in July and $22.7 in October (lmp_analysis_output.txt).

What follows: the same installed fleet can offer RMP a second product, a day-ahead scheduled evening block during forecast System Critical Hours, on top of frequency response. Up to a break point the tool computes for any fleet, it costs hosts none of their demand-charge savings.

What the demo proves:
- It backtests May 1 to Oct 25, 2026 on real EDAM prices and EIA CO2, with simulated host loads and events sampled from Torus's own 2025 distribution.
- It compares three policies and reports, for each: calls answered at full power, host demand-charge dollars, evening MWh delivered, CO2 shifted and Pulse cycles used.
- It plots the trade-off curve between block MW and host savings.
torus_tie:
How it feeds Torus revenue:

1) Wattsmart and Rocky Mountain Power, the proven engine.
- RMP covers the system cost, and the host pays a subscription starting at $549/month. The CEO says O&M fees are offset by bill savings and demand-response revenue (utah-grid.findings.md, torus-intel.findings.md).
- RampMeter raises what RMP gets per installed MW: frequency response all day, plus a forecast evening block from the same steel. That strengthens the case for filling the up-to-500 MW MOU (a ceiling, not installed capacity; the 70 MW agreement filled within six months) and for expanding the program.
- Its main output is a day-ahead operating envelope plus a list of System Critical Hours. In its June 2026 comments to the Western resource adequacy program (ROWE), Torus asked for exactly these: credit for "controlled and scheduled dispatch", standards for "aggregated and utility-directed operating envelopes", and System Critical Hours defined transparently (torus-intel.findings.md). A Torus exec can carry this to RMP's demand-side team and into that proceeding.
- Lasso already logs every past event for program expansion and IRP filings. RampMeter adds the forward-looking half.

2) Selling to C&I prospects.
- None of the 11 case studies publishes a system size or a measured saving (torus-cases-a/b.findings.md).
- The host one-pager puts a dollar figure on demand-charge savings (simulated, labeled). It also answers the objection a prospect will raise about sharing the battery: "no Rocky Mountain Power call cost you your monthly peak".
- Torus says demand charges are about 50% of a C&I bill and are set by the single highest 15- or 30-minute interval (torus-cases-a/b.findings.md).

3) Other territories at no extra cost.
- Torus's 2026 focus is the RMP, Pacific Power and PGE territories.
- PACE and PACW have been in EDAM since May 1 and PGE since Oct 1, 2026, and the same OASIS query works for ELAP_PACW-APND and ELAP_PGE-APND (tested, data-option1.findings.md). The adapter covers all three partners by changing the node name.

4) Data centers (Option 2 cameo).
- Torus pitches Spin for "AI training cycles", and Creekstone's Delta, Utah campus got Torus Load Smoothing on Dec 29, 2025 (torus-intel.findings.md).
- RampMeter treats a cluster as one more host, with a power-cap lane.

How it maps onto the hardware. Spin holds the RMP lane (10C, 6-minute full discharge, 25,000 cycles). Pulse works the host peak and the rush-hour block (0.5C, 7,500 cycles). That gives a concrete, physics-based reason the hybrid exists.

What is complementary and what Lasso already does. Per torus.co, Lasso already has:
- ML forecasting from load, weather and grid signals
- sub-250 ms dispatch
- routing of each event to Spin or Pulse
- savings quantification
- fleet VPP views
- a SCADA/DERMS/ADMS API
- an event audit log

RampMeter does no real-time control and does not rebuild any of that. It sits a day ahead and publishes hourly limits and setpoints that Lasso could carry out. None of the following is advertised on the 14+ Torus pages read:
- a grid-wide congestion and price forecast for PACE from open data (EDAM price with its congestion component, net load and ramp, CO2)
- an explicit utility-versus-host reservation, published to the utility as an envelope
- pricing Pulse cycle wear
- CO2 accounting
- plain-language reasons for each hour's plan
- compute as a controllable load

We will say "not advertised", never "Torus lacks". The output schema is shaped for IEEE 2030.5, the interface RMP requires (torus-cases-a.findings.md). The project uses its own brand and no Torus logos, and calls every station "simulated Torus-style (Spin + Pulse)".
demo_script:
The judging slot is Wed 5-6pm MT, and the evening rush hour on screen starts during it. Everything runs locally with DATA_MODE=snapshot, using the bundle frozen Tue night.

0:00-0:20 HOOK. Screen: title, then today's traffic strip, 24 colored hours.
- Say: "Torus's CTO describes grid congestion as the freeway at 5pm on a Friday. Utah's grid has a rush hour too, and it starts during this session. This is today's traffic report for PacifiCorp East, built last night from free CAISO and EIA data."

0:20-0:50 THE PREDICTABLE RUSH HOUR. Screen: the Traffic Report, with every chart labeled REAL.
- Day-ahead price with the congestion part shaded.
- Solar falling off a cliff.
- Load peak.
- CO2 forecast line (labeled DERIVED).
- Red window marked "System Critical Hours".
- Live 5-minute PACE real-time price ticker, with a "snapshot" badge if offline.
- Say (rehearsed with the Oct 27 numbers, swapped for Wednesday's): "Price goes from $21 at 3pm to $56 at 6pm as two gigawatts of solar disappear in two hours. The priciest hours this month ran 85% fossil."

0:50-1:20 THE RUSH HOUR YOU CAN'T PREDICT. Screen: Torus's own 2025 event heatmap (transcribed, labeled TORUS-PUBLISHED) laid over the traffic strip, with a time-zone toggle. Counters: 359 calls, 19-second ramp, ~5.5 minutes each, about 33 hours a year.
- Say: "Rocky Mountain Power calls these stations at every hour of the day. You can't forecast them. But each call needs power for about six minutes, and a full-power call uses less than 5% of a Pulse. Spin empties in six minutes. The utility's promise is a kilowatt promise."

1:20-2:00 THE PLAN. Screen: Fleet Lanes, 12 cards labeled SIMULATED (machine shop, steel fabricator, school with geothermal heat pumps, 24/7 dispatch center, grocery, office, packaging plant, AI cluster). Each card is a stacked area of three lanes through the day:
- teal: RMP lane on Spin
- blue: host-peak lane on Pulse, with the host's demand ceiling as a dashed line
- amber: rush-hour lane
A fleet bar reads "RMP lane: X MW all day. Scheduled block: Y MW, 6-9pm." Hover any hour for its reason in plain words, e.g. "Holding 250 kW on Spin for RMP; Pulse delivering 300 kW because 6pm is $55.78 and solar is 36 MW."

2:00-2:30 WOW. Click "RMP calls at 6:12pm". Split screen, naive policy against RampMeter, 1-second playback:
- Spin ramps in 19 s and carries the call.
- Pulse keeps delivering the block.
- The host's 15-minute meter stays under its ceiling, and the refill waits for the green midday window.
- On the naive side, the refill lands in the host's peak interval and sets a new monthly peak (red "+$ demand charge", tariff assumption labeled).
- Then the Backtest tab: May-Oct 2026 on real prices, three policies, table plus the trade-off curve between block MW and host savings. Point to its break point: "The first Y MW of evening block cost these hosts nothing."

2:30-2:50 OPTION 2 IN ONE BREATH. Screen: the AI-cluster card.
- Say: "Compute is just another host. Cap the GPUs at 300 watts from 6 to 9 and you keep 86-95% of throughput (Emerald AI's public data). Pulse is freed for the grid. Compute follows the sun, and the station covers the cliff."

2:50-3:00 CLOSE. Screen: Export, showing the RMP envelope one-pager and the host one-pager.
- Say: "Lasso runs the second. RampMeter plans the day. Same steel, second paycheck. It works for Rocky Mountain Power, Pacific Power and PGE tomorrow, because all three are in the same day-ahead market."
wow_moment:
Injecting a Rocky Mountain Power call at 6:12pm, live, in the middle of the evening rush hour shown on the traffic strip. The split screen replays it second by second:
- RampMeter: Spin ramps in 19 seconds and carries the 5.5-minute call alone. Pulse never stops delivering the scheduled block. The host's 15-minute demand meter stays flat under its ceiling. Spin's refill is held until the green midday window (or comes from Pulse, if Torus confirms that is possible).
- The naive "host-first, refill immediately" policy, same call: the rebound draw sets a new monthly demand peak and a red dollar penalty appears.

Then the pull-back. The backtest over 178 real EDAM days shows this holds across thousands of sampled calls, and the trade-off curve shows how many evening MW Torus can offer RMP before any host pays for it.

It lands because Torus judges see their own 19-second ramp and their own event heatmap driving the simulation, and the rush hour on screen is the one outside the building during judging (a live 5-minute PACE price ticker, falling back to the snapshot).
architecture:
Repo layout, one owner per directory:
- contracts/: pydantic models exported to JSON Schema and generated TS types. Objects: GridHour, TrafficReport, EventRiskHour, StationSpec, Site, PlanInterval, FleetPlan, EventScenario, BacktestResult, Envelope, Provenance{label: REAL|DERIVED|SIMULATED|TORUS-PUBLISHED, source, pulled_at}.
- data/: one adapter per source.
  - oasis.py: PRC_LMP DAM, SLD_FCST DAM, EDAM_WND_SLR_FORECAST_GRP XML, PRC_INTVL_LMP RTM
  - eia930.py: six-month balance CSVs filtered to PACE
  - eia_co2.py: PACE.xlsx parsed once to parquet
  - openmeteo.py
  - snapshot.py: builds dated bundles
  - cache/: committed parquet and JSON
- engine/: stress.py, co2_model.py, events.py, fleet.py (archetypes and load synthesis), planner.py (LP), policies.py (baselines and the real-time rule), simulate.py, backtest.py, explain.py, envelope.py.
- api/: FastAPI.
  - GET /traffic?date
  - GET /events/risk?date&tz_preset
  - POST /plan {fleet_id, block_mw, cycle_budget, tz_preset}
  - POST /simulate {plan_id, event_at, policy}
  - GET /backtest
  - GET /envelope/{date}.json
  - GET /onepager/{rmp|host}/{site}
- app/: Vite + React + TypeScript + ECharts. Five screens: Traffic Report, Calls (heatmap), Fleet Lanes, Event Replay, Backtest/Frontier, plus Export. Big type for a room, dark and light themes, a provenance badge on every chart.
- demo/: script.md, rehearsal timings, backup video.

Data flow: adapters write a normalized hourly table keyed on UTC interval start (OASIS is GMT with Pacific hour-ending, EIA is Mountain local, Open-Meteo is whatever zone you request; data-option1.md says join on UTC). From that, snapshot.py writes bundles/{date}/ (traffic.json, history.parquet, co2_coef.json). The engine reads only bundles, the API serves engine output, and the UI reads only the API. MDT is UTC-6 until Nov 1, after judging.

Precomputed offline:
- PACE history May 1-Oct 26, 2026 (EDAM prices) and Jul 2025-Oct 2026 (EIA)
- CO2 regression coefficients
- the full backtest and the frontier sweep, cached JSON regenerated by a script
- the demo-day bundle for Wed Oct 28, frozen Tue night, with Oct 27 kept as backup

Live during the demo:
- the planner solve when a slider moves (about 7k LP variables for 12 sites x 96 intervals, sub-second with HiGHS; estimate, to be measured)
- event-injection simulation
- an optional live RTM 5-minute price fetch, server-side, with a 5-second timeout and fallback to the snapshot (OASIS has no CORS and allows about 1 request per 5 s)

Runs on the laptop: uvicorn plus vite preview. A static export of the precomputed JSON is the fallback if Python dies.

DATA_MODE=snapshot|live, default snapshot, shown as an on-screen "Snapshot as of <timestamp>" badge.

Secrets: none needed. Every source is keyless.

core_algorithms:
1) Grid Stress Index and System Critical Hours (about 3h).
- For each hour: z-scores over the trailing 30 days of DA LMP (weight 0.4), net load (0.3), 3-hour net-load ramp (0.2) and CO2 forecast (0.1). The weights are a design choice, shown in a tooltip.
- Map to 0-100 and to Green/Yellow/Red/Black. The top-K contiguous Red hours are the System Critical Hours (K is a slider, default 3).
- Validate May-Oct 2026: how often the day-ahead Red window contains the realized EIA net-load peak hour and the day's top-3 price hours. Report the hit rate on screen.

2) Tomorrow's CO2 (about 2h).
- Ridge regression of EIA hourly PACE CO2 intensity on solar MW, wind MW, demand MW, hour of day and month, trained on EIA actuals Jul 2025-Sep 2026 and held out on Oct 2026. Report MAE.
- Apply to the EDAM solar/wind forecast and the SLD_FCST load to forecast tomorrow. This is the recommendation in data-option1.md.

3) Frequency-call risk model (about 2h).
- lambda(day, hour) = (h_k/359) x (7 x w_dow/359) x (12 x m_month/356) x 359/365, expected calls in that slot. This uses the Torus hourly, weekday and approximate monthly marginals.
- Arrivals: Poisson thinning. Duration Uniform(5, 6) minutes. 19-s linear ramp to 100% of enrolled kW, matching the trace's band.
- Time-zone preset: as-published, or shifted from UTC. Everything downstream is reported under both to show the plan is robust.

4) Reservation planner, a 15-minute LP over 24-48h solved for the whole fleet with cvxpy + HiGHS (about 6h).
- Per site and interval, variables: Pulse charge c, Pulse discharge d, grid import g, export x (allowed during events and the block), Pulse state of charge e, and the month-to-date peak P.
- Constraints:
  - load balance g - x = L + c - d
  - state of charge with efficiencies (assumption 0.92 one-way)
  - Pulse power at most 0.5C x E
  - RMP power lane: Spin_kW + (Pmax - d) >= R_ffr in every interval
  - RMP energy lane: Spin_kWh + (e - e_min) >= R_ffr x 6/60
  - refill headroom: P - g >= rho x R_spin_refill in the host's peak-window intervals
  - P >= g and P >= peak already set this month
  - a fleet block constraint during System Critical Hours: sum over sites of (L - g + x) >= B_t
  - Pulse throughput within a daily cycle budget derived from 7,500 cycles over 25 years (slider)
- Objective: minimize host energy cost + demand charge x P + wear cost x throughput.
- The block B is swept from 0 to the maximum to draw the trade-off curve between block MW and host savings. The break point is the "free MW" number.

5) Real-time rule and simulator, numpy at 1-second steps inside call windows and 15-minute steps elsewhere (about 4h).
- When a call arrives: Spin first, then Pulse's spare power.
- After the call: refill Spin, either internally from Pulse (option, to confirm with Torus) or from the grid capped at P - g, and never during Red hours unless Spin falls below its floor.
- Bill on 15-minute average import.
- Three policies:
  - A, utility-first: hold 80% charge for RMP always
  - B, host-first: greedy peak shaving, refill immediately
  - C, RampMeter: the LP plan plus the rule
- Monte Carlo of 200 call scenarios per day.
- Outputs: share of calls delivered at full power and on time, change in host demand charge, MWh delivered to the block, CO2 shifted (EIA hourly intensity at charge versus discharge hours, average basis, labeled), Pulse and Spin equivalent full cycles per year (simple throughput count; rainflow is a stretch).

6) Backtest (about 3h).
- 178 EDAM days (May 1-Oct 25, 2026) x 12 sites x 3 policies, each day planned only on that day's day-ahead data, with monthly demand-charge settlement. Runs in minutes and is cached.

7) Explainer and envelope (about 2h).
- Plain-language reasons are deterministic templates, no LLM: they fill in the binding constraint and the driving signal.
- Envelope JSON per hour: {start_utc, local, stress, critical_hour, ffr_kw_ready, ffr_kw_ready_p95, scheduled_kw, reason, provenance}, shaped for IEEE 2030.5 DER control schedules (an assumption about the schema shape).
- Two printable one-pagers, RMP and host.

8) Option 2 load class (about 2h).
- The AI-cluster site gets a curtailment variable u_t, capped at deferrable share x load.
- Its cost comes from Emerald's throughput-versus-cap curve, with dollars per lost GPU-hour as a labeled assumption. It also gets an optional 12-hour deferral window.

Total engine estimate: about 24 agent-assisted hours, run in parallel lanes.

name: Crossover
one_liner: Crossover splits an AI campus's power draw into three time bands and gives each band to the machine that wears least doing it. Torus Spin takes the sub-second training swings, Torus Pulse takes PacifiCorp East's multi-hour rush-hour events, and the GPUs flex only for what is left. The schedule comes from tomorrow's open day-ahead grid forecast.
the_insight:
An AI campus is three different loads at three timescales, and each resource is cheap at exactly one of them. The winning design gives the battery none of the swing, and gives the GPUs none of a grid event until the battery is empty. The numbers, with sources:

1) SECONDS
- Training power concentrates at 0.2-3 Hz (Microsoft/OpenAI/NVIDIA arXiv 2508.14318; prior-art.findings.md).
- NVIDIA's rack capacitors hold 65 J per GPU, about 1.8 kWh per 100k GPUs, so nothing on the rack covers a 1-2 second half-swing (data-option2.findings.md).
- Our 50 Hz simulation (SIMULATED): a 300 MW campus with 60% of its load in one synchronized job, swinging 40-100% at 0.5 Hz. The 40-100% range is from the ERCOT Aug 2025 deck.
- If a Pulse sized for grid events (200 MWh, 0.5C) also absorbs the swing, it sees about 42,000 oscillations and 2.95 equivalent full cycles a day. That is about 7 years to its 7,500-cycle rating, against about 19 years doing one arbitrage cycle a day plus curtailment. The 7 years is the same order of magnitude as Torus's own claim that AI workloads wear out chemical batteries in 3-5 years.
- Spin (10C) handles the band with energy to spare. It needs about 105 MW of power but only 0.81 MWh of swing at a 30 s crossover, against about 10.5 MWh of 10C capacity. Grid-side content in the 0.5-5 Hz local-swing band falls from 38 to 0.35 MW rms.

2) HOURS
- PACE's capacity rush hour is real but rare. We reran the Duke "Rethinking Load Growth" method (annual-peak ceiling; our implementation; DERIVED) on 12 months of EIA-930 PACE demand, Oct 26 2025 to Oct 25 2026. The peak in that window is 10,173 MW on Jul 20 2026.
- Result: about 1.27 GW of headroom at 0.5% curtailment. Duke's chart reads about 1.5 GW.
- Every curtailed hour falls in June to August, hour-ending 12-22, and 90% of those hours need at most half of the new load curtailed. Duke's national figure is 88%.
- Utah's grid-connected data-center build is 902 MW (2,602 MW under construction minus 1,700 MW behind the meter or off-grid, per the 2026 legislative brief in utah-grid.findings.md). It would need curtailment in only 61 hours a year (0.17%), across 22 events.
- The worst event is Jul 20 2026: 8 hours, noon to 8pm, 4,355 MWh.

3) THE GPUs
- Emerald's public sweep: capping A100s at 300 W keeps 86-95% of throughput (emerald/dvfs_sweep.csv). Compute flex is expensive per MWh but has no duration limit.
- Take a 300 MW campus as a pro-rata slice of the 902 MW cohort. A 100 MW / 200 MWh Pulse covers 13 of 22 events with no GPU action, and covers 50% of the 4,498 MWh a year of curtailment.
- The remaining 2,249 MWh a year (0.09% of the campus's maximum annual energy) goes to job deferral first and power caps last.

So the load a legislative brief calls non-interruptible can be made interruptible for PacifiCorp East, with the GPUs untouched on most event days, as long as the bands never mix.

The boundary between Spin and compute comes down to one number: how Spin's 25,000-cycle rating counts micro-cycles. On the same simulated trace:
- counting every swing as a cycle gives Spin 14 hours of life;
- counting throughput gives 1.2 years;
- rainflow plus Miner fatigue (S-N exponent 3, an assumption) gives effectively unlimited life.

The alternative is to raise the GPU power floor from 40% to 70% to halve the swing. That burns 518 MWh a day, $5.9-7.2M a year at real PACE day-ahead prices (July 2026 mean $31.01; Oct 27 mean $38.22).

Reproduce: scratch-depth/headroom.py, bandsplit.py and extras.py, with their *_output.txt files, under <research scratchpad>/research/

A monorepo with four directories, each owned by one lane. Python engine, TypeScript UI. Everything the stage demo needs is precomputed into committed JSON bundles.

- Every record carries provenance {kind: REAL|DERIVED|SIMULATED, source, pulled_at, note}.

data/ (adapters; one file per source; server-side only)
- oasis.py: PRC_LMP DAM and RTM 5-min, SLD_FCST DAM, and the EDAM_WND_SLR GroupZip XML. Paced 5 s apart, under 31 days per call, unzipped.
- eia930.py: six-month CSVs filtered to PACE.

- traffic.py: net load, stress probability, CO2 forecast, event-risk prior.
- plan.py: day-ahead hourly LP producing the DispatchPlan.

- wear.py: rainflow counting and three Spin wear models plus an LFP model.

core_algorithms:
A) TRAFFIC REPORT (Option 1, hourly, 24-48 hours ahead)
- Inputs per hour: day-ahead LMP and congestion component, load forecast, solar and wind forecasts.
- Net load = load minus solar minus wind.
- Rush score = weighted percentile ranks of LMP, net-load 3-hour ramp, and forecast CO2.
- Stress probability: p(h) = P(D_fcst(h) x (1+e) + L_new > ceiling), with e bootstrapped from 11,473 hourly EIA day-ahead errors.
- CO2: a ridge regression fit on the last 90 days of PACE.xlsx.
- RMP event risk: a fixed hourly prior from the 359-event heatmap. It cannot be forecast, so it becomes a reserve rather than a schedule; that is the torus-cases-a insight.

The forecast feeds the stack in four ways:
1. p(h) sets the hours when Pulse must be full and compute deferral pre-armed.
2. Price and CO2 shape set the Pulse arbitrage windows and the compute envelope, a Google-style hourly "virtual capacity curve".
3. The event prior sets a constant SoC reserve.
4. Net-load ramp and stress set an hourly grid ramp limit R(h) and crossover time constant tau(h). Spin works harder only when the grid is jammed, citing NVIDIA's note that generation takes 1 to 90 minutes to follow ramps.

B) DAY-AHEAD PLAN (LP, about 200 variables, HiGHS)
- Variables per hour: Pulse charge, discharge and SoC; deferred energy moved in and out; power-cap shed x_h; grid draw g_h.
- Constraints:
  - SoC dynamics with round-trip efficiency;
  - 0.5C power limit;
  - reserve floor <= SoC <= capacity;
  - deferrable energy conserved within a deadline window;
  - shed <= 25% of non-deferrable load (the Emerald field-test level);
  - in curtailment hours, g_h <= campus power minus the required curtailment;
  - g_h = load - shed - net deferral + charge - discharge.
- Objective: sum of LMP x g + optional carbon price x CI x g + Pulse wear price x throughput + a convex piecewise shed cost (Emerald curve x GPU-hour value) + a small deferral penalty.
- Output: the DispatchPlan JSON.
- Fallback if time is short: a greedy rule in wear order (defer, then Pulse, then caps).

C) BAND-SPLIT SIMULATION (50 Hz, 10-minute windows at chosen hours, about 30k samples)
- Grid target = EMA(load, tau).
- Spin power = load - target + k(SoC_target - SoC). Clipped to Spin power and SoC limits.
- Ramp limiter: when |dg/dt| > R(h), Spin absorbs the excess.
- Pulse tracks the plan setpoint and absorbs Spin's SoC-restoring power, within its 0.5C limit.
- Compute's fast lever: the GPU power floor f, which raises comm-phase power and burns energy.
- RMP event injection: Spin carries the first seconds and Pulse carries the 5-6 minutes, or Spin if its SoC allows. The trace is drawn like Torus's own event chart.

D) WEAR (wear.py)
- Turning points, then ASTM 3-point rainflow on the SoC traces.
- Three Spin models:
  1. count every oscillation;
  2. throughput equivalent full cycles (discharged energy / capacity);
  3. fatigue: Miner's sum of n_i x (range_i / capacity)^m with an endurance threshold.
- Pulse: throughput equivalent full cycles with a depth-dependent life curve N(DoD) = 7,500 x DoD^-k.
- Outputs: cycles a year, life in years, and a wear price per year from sliders. The scratch prototype already runs in under 10 s for 2 hours at 50 Hz.

E) COMPLIANCE
- Welch spectrum of grid draw (120 s segments).
- RMS per band, using the ERCOT risk bands: under 0.5 Hz inter-area, 0.5-5 Hz local swing mode, 5-25 Hz torsional (limited by the Nyquist frequency at 50 Hz sampling).
- Share of variance in 0.1-20 Hz against an illustrative cap.
- Maximum ramp in MW/s, and dynamic range over 1 s and 60 s windows.
- Pass/fail chips.

F) WEAR-PRICED CROSSOVER (crossover.py)
- Grid search over tau in {2, 5, 10, 30, 60, 120, 300} s, floor f in {40, 55, 70, 85}% and 3 Spin wear models.
- Minimize annualized Spin wear + Pulse wear + burner energy (simulated MW x real LMP), subject to compliance and to Spin energy <= its 10C capacity (tau <= roughly 6 minutes).
- Display the cost curve, the chosen point, and the boundary where the choice flips between wear models.

G) HEADROOM (headroom.py, already prototyped)
- Binary search for new load L where curtailment / (L x hours) = r, with ceiling = the window maximum (annual) or the season maximum.
- Event extraction, durations, month-by-hour heatmap.
- Pulse coverage curve against MW at 0.5C (2 hours).
- Residual per event assigned to deferral, then caps.

SIZED FOR 44 HOURS
- A, C, D, E and G are each roughly 100-300 lines, and two of them already run in scratch.
- B is the riskiest piece and has the greedy fallback.
- F is a loop over C, D and E.

Both, with Option 2 as the spine.

Option 2 ("compute follows the sun"):
- A job router across four real EDAM nodes: ELAP_PACE, ELAP_PACW, ELAP_PGE and the TH_SP15 hub.
- It picks where and when each deferrable AI block runs, using three signals: day-ahead price (REAL), carbon intensity (DERIVED) and grid stress (DERIVED from the EDAM load and wind/solar forecasts).
- It shows cost and CO2 saved against honest baselines: stay put, time-only, place-only and carbon-only.

Option 1 ("rush hour for electrons"):

the_insight:
HEADLINE: Software can pick the hour; only storage can absorb the second. A price-smart router does not remove Utah's grid risk, it imports it. The AI work that can move is training, the load that swings in seconds. Every router reading the same day-ahead price lands that work in Utah and pulls it out at the same top of the hour.

Where the numbers come from:
- Prices: REAL CAISO OASIS EDAM day-ahead LMPs, pulled 2026-10-26.
- Carbon: DERIVED from the EIA-930 fuel mix times IPCC AR5 medians. These factors come from utah-grid.findings.md; oil 650 and other 230 g/kWh are my assumptions.
- Computed in <research scratchpad>/research/scratch-opt2/ (where_vs_when_output.txt, carbon_tradeoff_output.txt, step_hours_output.txt).

1) MONEY MOVES IN TIME (Oct 1-27, 2026)
- Utah (PACE) was the cheapest PacifiCorp/PGE node in 81% of 648 hours.
- At Utah's priciest hour each day, the cheapest other PacifiCorp/PGE node was a median $0.10/MWh cheaper. With California's SP15 hub included, it was $1.80.
- Utah's own daily max-min spread was a median $23.50/MWh.
- Take a 4-hour evening block (5-9pm MDT, 23 complete days):
  - waiting for Utah's cheapest 4 hours cut cost 40%;
  - moving to the cheapest node at the same hours cut it 8%.
- July (PACE/PACW/SP15): 51% versus 13%.
- This matches Sukprasert et al. (prior-art): simple time-shifting captures most of the value.

2) CARBON MOVES IN PLACE
- PACE was both cheaper and dirtier than PACW in 456 of 576 October hours.
- At every hour I sampled, PACE's derived intensity ran 124-269 g/kWh above PACW's (PACE 378-566, PACW 251-356).
- The cheapest node was also the cleanest in only 15% of October hours.
- Price-only routing keeps 89% of block-hours in Utah: cost -41%, CO2 -29%.
- Adding a $25/t CO2 weight keeps the cost saving (-40%), cuts CO2 by 44% and drops Utah's share to 51%.
- Median PACE-versus-PACW break-even: $31/t in October, $2/t in July (the two prices nearly match in July).

3) THE EXIT IS SYNCHRONIZED
- On 24 of 27 October days, the day's largest upward PACE price step came at 5pm or 6pm MDT (median +$15.10/MWh).
- That step sits on the steepest part of PACE's net-load climb. October mean net load (EIA-930 derived) rose from 2,905 MW at 4pm to 4,024 MW at 7pm. The summer average 3-hour ramp was +1,031 MW (utah-grid.findings.md).
- Europe has seen this pattern under hourly schedules. Frequency swings cluster around the hour, which is one reason its day-ahead market moved to 15-minute blocks on Oct 1, 2025. Sources: the ENTSO-E/Eurelectric 2012 deterministic-frequency-deviation report and arXiv 2602.09645. I saw these only through a search summary and did not read them on source.

4) THE WORK THAT MOVES IS THE WORK THAT SHAKES (inferred)
- The deferrable job classes are training and offline batch work, per the Alibaba v2026 HP/LP priority and job_type labels. Latency-bound inference, as in the Azure LLM trace, cannot move.
- Training power concentrates at 0.2-3 Hz, with swings of tens to hundreds of MW (Microsoft/OpenAI/NVIDIA 2025).
- On-rack capacitors hold 65 J/GPU, about 1.8 kWh per 100,000 GPUs.

SO, BY TIMESCALE
- Hours (where and when): software. This is the router.
- The top-of-hour cliff: also software. Slewing a 40 MW exit evenly across the boundary costs about $19 at the median October step (illustrative arithmetic: 1.25 MWh shifted x $15.10).
- Seconds: the training swing, and RMP fast-frequency calls (19 s ramp, 359 events in 2025).
- One to two hours: the inflexible base through the evening.
- Those last two are storage, which is exactly where Torus Spin and Pulse sit.
torus_tie:
The pitch says this out loud: Torus does not route compute, and the router is not proposed as a Torus product.
- torus-intel.findings.md infers that Torus has no cross-region compute product.
- Hour-scale shifting needs no storage. Emerald cut a 256-GPU cluster 25% for 3 hours with software only (prior-art.findings.md).
- The router is the context that creates demand for Torus. The landing is Torus's lane.

WHERE TORUS FITS
- Spin (10C, full discharge in 6 minutes, 25,000 cycles) absorbs the 0.2-3 Hz training swing and answers fast-frequency calls.
- Pulse (0.5C, 7,500 cycles) carries the inflexible inference base through 6-8pm and holds reserve for Rocky Mountain Power (RMP) calls. Utility Dive cites Pulse from 270 kWh to 2.2 MWh, expandable to 40 MWh.
- Torus already pitched this for data centers: swings of tens of MW within seconds, and sub-synchronous oscillations. It installed "Torus Load Smoothing" at Creekstone's Delta, Utah AI campus on Dec 29, 2025 (torus-intel.findings.md).

THE ROUTER'S MAP IS TORUS'S SALES MAP
- PACE (Rocky Mountain Power), PACW (Pacific Power) and PGE are all EDAM members.
- All three are named Torus utility territories in the CEO's 2026 priorities.
- So whichever of the three the router picks, the landing site is in Torus territory. California is the one region on the map that is not.

REVENUE HOOKS
1. Data-center hardware plus subscription, sized by the landing plan. The MW of training landed sets Spin MW, and the evening base sets Pulse MWh. This is a self-serve sizing view; torus-cases-b lists self-serve sizing as not advertised, since design is a human service.
2. RMP flexible capacity. A flexible AI campus behind a Torus Station is dispatchable capacity of the Wattsmart kind: 359 VPP events in 2025, under an MOU of up to 500 MW. Say "up to"; it is a ceiling, not installed capacity.
3. A new input for Lasso. The router publishes the campus's next-day flexible-load plan on the evening EDAM clears (about 9:15pm MT). Lasso cannot forecast that from load, weather and grid signals, because it is a scheduling decision. Lasso's pages mention no compute-scheduler integration.
4. Utah policy fit. SB 132's first large-load contract (PSC 26-035-05, more than 100 MW) values the customer's energy hourly at the EDAM price near the load. The router's signal is the settlement signal. The customer's own tariff is confidential, so do not claim it pays the EDAM price.

COMPLEMENTARY VS WHAT LASSO ALREADY DOES
- Lasso already claims:
  - ML forecasting from load, weather and grid signals;
  - routing each event between Spin and Pulse;
  - dispatch in under 250 ms;
  - VPP performance logs;
  - a SCADA/DERMS/ADMS API.
- We do not claim the Spin/Pulse split. Our controller is a labeled stand-in.
- What is new:
  - routing intent across regions as a Lasso input;
  - a carbon signal (not advertised as a Lasso input);
  - a timescale breakdown showing what software can do and what needs storage;
  - sizing per MW of landed training;
  - an explicit reserve held for random RMP calls while Pulse also works the evening.

core_algorithms:
1) CARBON (Python, about 60 LOC)
- Formula: CI_r(h) = sum over fuels of max(Gen_f,0) x EF_f, divided by sum over fuels of max(Gen_f,0).
- IPCC AR5 medians: coal 820, gas 490, solar 48, wind 11, hydro 24, geothermal 38, nuclear 12 g/kWh. Oil 650 and other 230 are my assumptions.
- Validate PACE against EIA's PACE.xlsx direct intensity.
- Demo-day forecast:
  - per BA, the hour-of-day median over the last 14 days;
  - for PACE, plus a least-squares correction on EDAM solar and wind shares, fit on October;
  - report MAE on held-out days.

2) STRESS (TS, about 40 LOC)
- Net load = load forecast minus wind forecast minus solar forecast, per region.
- stress(h) = 0.6 x within-day rank of net load + 0.4 x rank of the next-hour upramp, scaled 0-1.

3) ROUTER (TS, about 200 LOC)
- Decision variable: x[j,r,h] MWh.
- Minimize the sum of x x (price[r,h] + lambdaC x CI[r,h]/1000 + lambdaS x stress[r,h] x Pref).
- Constraints:
  - each job's energy is met;
  - each job's max MW is respected;
  - each job runs inside its window;
  - region landing capacity: cap[r,h] = site MW minus the inflexible base;
  - a soft anti-herding penalty on the boundary step |load[r,h+1] - load[r,h]| above a cap.
- Method:
  - greedy marginal-cost fill, which is exact for the transport form;
  - then a local-search pass for the boundary term;
  - plus the baselines (stay, time-only, place-only, carbon-only) so the UI reproduces the insight table;
  - optional javascript-lp-solver for the exact solve.

4) SLEW (TS, about 40 LOC)
- A linear exit over the window [b - w/2, b + w/2].
- Cost delta = energy shifted across the boundary x price step. Throughput is unchanged.
- Alternative power-cap slew priced on Emerald's throughput-versus-cap curve.

5) LANDING SIM (TS, about 300 LOC)
- Two views:
  - 2 h at 1 s, with the oscillation shown as an RMS band;
  - 60 s at 50 Hz, enough to resolve 0.2-3 Hz and run an FFT up to 25 Hz.
- Campus load = inference base + training from the router plan x (1 - a x smoothed-square(2 x pi x f x t)), plus a checkpoint dip every N minutes.
- Torus stand-in:
  - grid target = ramp-rate-limited low-pass of load (tau 60 s, Rmax slider);
  - residual r = load minus target;
  - Spin takes the high-pass of r (tau 10 s); Pulse takes the rest;
  - clamp to power and state-of-charge limits; any shortfall goes to the grid and is flagged;
  - 90% round-trip efficiency (assumption);
  - Pulse keeps SoC at or above the reserve (slider; default is the energy for one 6-minute call at event power).
- Evening mode: Pulse charges in the cheapest midday hours and discharges 6-8pm against the inference base. Report cost and CO2 deltas, with DERIVED labels.

6) RMP EVENTS (TS, about 50 LOC)
- Inhomogeneous Poisson arrivals scaled to 359 per year, using Torus's published hour-of-day counts (toggle: local or UTC).
- Each event lasts 5-6 minutes and must deliver within the 30 s target.
- Fallback when reserve is short: compute shed at 40% per minute (the EPRI UK test). Report served or missed.

7) METRICS (TS, about 120 LOC)
- Max 1-minute ramp in MW/min.
- FFT band energy over 0.1-20 Hz (Hann window, 2,048 points) against an example cap. The cap is an assumption, in the style of the Microsoft/OpenAI/NVIDIA spec.
- Pulse equivalent full cycles per year = throughput / (2 x E) x 365, against 7,500.
- Spin depth-weighted half-cycles via a simple rainflow count, against 25,000, with a caveat on screen.

8) INSIGHT STATS (Python, plus a TS twin with vitest pins)
- Pinned values: 81%, $0.10, $23.50, -40% vs -8%, 15%, 89% to 51%, 24 of 27 days, $15.10, $31/t.
- If a data refresh changes a number, the test fails loudly, so the pitch never quotes stale figures.

Total: about 900 TS LOC plus about 400 Python LOC, which fits two agent lanes across one working day.

name: Clearlane
one_liner: Tomorrow's traffic report for Utah's grid: every night it reads the new western day-ahead market and plans each Torus Station to fill up in the clear lane, empty into rush hour, and keep a shoulder lane open for the crash nobody can predict.
options_covered:
Both, with Option 1 as the spine.
- Option 1 (rush hour for electrons): a day-ahead traffic report for PacifiCorp East built from real CAISO EDAM data (price, congestion component, load, solar and wind forecasts), plus a plan that keeps a simulated fleet of Torus-style stations out of traffic. Pulse charges in the clear lane and discharges into the jam. Spin holds a crash lane for unplanned Rocky Mountain Power calls at every hour.
- Option 2 (compute follows the sun): a 100 MW AI campus joins the same map as "a truck that can wait". It defers 25% of its load for 3 hours, the depth Emerald AI showed on real GPUs (prior-art.findings #1), and Spin smooths the step. A single "where" card compares tomorrow's real day-ahead prices at PACE, PACW, PGE and California's SP15 hub, all from the same OASIS pull (data-option1.findings #9; on Oct 27, SP15 was $9.14 at 10am against PACE's $23.23).

the_insight:
Utah's grid now publishes its rush hour a day ahead, and the "off-peak" everyone assumes is upside down. Crashes still can't be predicted, so a Torus Station should split the two jobs by physics.

1. The timetable is public. Since EDAM went live on May 1, 2026, every hour of tomorrow's PacifiCorp East (PACE) price is published the evening before. Oct 27's prices were already up by about 9:16pm MT on Oct 26 (data-option1.findings #2, #3; utah-grid.findings #1).

2. What the Oct 27 timetable shows (snapshot CSV; net load derived):
- Clear lane: 9am-5pm at $21.38-28.61/MWh, while about 2.2 GW of solar runs.
- Jam: 6pm-10pm at $54.57-55.78, which is 2.6x the low. Solar falls from 2,056 MW at 4pm to 36 MW at 6pm, and net load (load minus solar minus wind) climbs 3,655 MW between 3pm and 6pm.
- The overnight "off-peak" (1am-5am) averages $38.71/MWh, 70% more than 9am-4pm ($22.83).

3. EIA's own hourly CO2 for PACE agrees (PACE.xlsx, generated basis, parsed in scratch co2.py). Oct 1-25: about 698 g/kWh from 1am to 6am, 665 from 6pm to 10pm, 468 from 9am to 4pm. July: 751, 636 and 480.

4. The before/after the demo proves (scratch habit.py; Oct 27 day-ahead prices, EIA October hourly CO2):
- Setup: 70 MW of storage, the size of RMP's first Torus MOU (torus-cases-a.findings #3), discharging 6-8pm either way.
- Charged overnight out of habit: it earns $1,405 a day and ADDS about 18 t of CO2 a day.
- Charged in the published clear lane: it earns $4,088 a day (2.9x) and REMOVES about 19 t.
- Assumptions: a 2-hour, 0.5C battery, 88% round trip, and average rather than marginal emissions. The "adds CO2" result holds even at 100% round trip, because overnight power here is dirtier than the evening power it replaces.

5. What no timetable shows is the crash. Torus answered 359 RMP calls in 2025. Each ramped in 19 seconds and lasted about 5-6 minutes, and they fell across every hour of the day (torus-cases-a.findings #1, #8, #10).

6. So the plan splits the jobs:
- Pulse (0.5C, a 2-hour tank) follows the timetable.
- Spin (10C, full discharge in 6 minutes) holds a crash lane at all hours. A 5-6 minute call fits inside Spin's 6-minute tank (torus-cases-b.findings #9, #10).

7. Annual value. On July and October 2026 EDAM prices, the optimized one-cycle-a-day plan is worth $39.71-48.52 per MW-day (Oct 27 alone: $57.54). That is about $14,500-17,700 per MW-year (derived in scratch fix.py), roughly $1.0-1.2M a year for 70 MW and $7-9M at the up-to-500 MW MOU ceiling.

8. Cost of the crash lane. Holding it on a battery alone (a 0.1 MWh/MW floor plus 25% power headroom, both assumptions) costs about 3% of that value in my model. On a hybrid, Spin holds it and Pulse's plan is untouched.
torus_tie:
Torus is the hero hardware and Clearlane is the route plan. The pitch line: Torus builds the parking garages for electrons at the exits, and Clearlane tells every garage when to fill and when to empty. It extends the CTO's own image of power as a freeway at 5pm on a Friday, with electrons stored near the load while the road is clear (torus-intel.findings #2).

How it plugs in, product by product:
- Pulse, Spin and Lasso. Pulse works the published timetable and Spin holds the crash lane. Clearlane emits a nightly JSON plan for each station: hourly charge and discharge targets, a reserve floor, and a plain-language note. Lasso could take it as one more "grid signal" through its API library. Lasso already forecasts from load patterns, weather and grid signals, and connects to SCADA, DERMS and ADMS (torus-cases-b.findings #11). Torus's congestion-relief page says smaller utilities and co-ops let Torus schedule against forecasts through Lasso (torus-cases-a.findings #28). Clearlane is that forecast, built from open data.
- Rocky Mountain Power and Wattsmart. RMP calls the fleet in under 1% of hours (torus-cases-a.findings #4), and Wattsmart Battery plans already allow daily load cycling (peak management) alongside frequency reserve (torus-cases-a.findings #9). Clearlane prices the other 99% of hours, about $14,500-17,700 per MW-year at 2026 EDAM prices (derived). That is the case for growing from the 70 MW first MOU toward the up-to-500 MW MOU (torus-cases-a.findings #3).
- Three territories in one feed. Torus's 2026 focus is RMP, Pacific Power and PGE (torus-intel.findings #8). EDAM has covered PACE and PACW since May 1 and PGE since Oct 1 (utah-grid.findings #1), and one OASIS call returns all three nodes (data-option1.findings #9). Clearlane works in every Torus territory on day one, with no API keys.
- Host sales. No case study publishes a system size or a measured saving (torus-cases-a.findings #24; torus-cases-b.findings #6). The "your station tomorrow" card gives a rep a labeled number. It respects the host's demand ceiling: one 15-minute window sets the month's demand charge, and demand charges are about 50% of a C&I bill (torus-cases-b.findings #27; torus-cases-a.findings #31).
- Data centers. Creekstone's Delta AI campus has run Torus Load Smoothing since Dec 29, 2025 (torus-intel.findings #13). Utah's first SB 132 data-center contract credits energy hourly at the EDAM price near the load (utah-grid.findings #21), the exact price Clearlane reads. Spin's FAQ already pitches covering AI training cycles (torus-cases-b.findings #9).
- Revenue. Torus sells energy-as-a-service through utility programs and host subscriptions. The CEO says O&M fees are typically offset by bill savings and demand-response revenue (torus-intel.findings #19). More dollars per installed MW makes each utility deal, each MOU expansion and each host subscription easier to sell.

Complementary, not a Lasso rebuild:
- Lasso already claims ML forecasting, sub-250 ms dispatch, Spin/Pulse event routing, VPP performance views and an auditable event log (torus-cases-b.findings #11; torus-cases-a.findings #27). Clearlane does none of that and never claims the Spin/Pulse split as new (prior-art.findings #19).
- It adds what Torus's pages do not advertise. That is absence from a marketing page, not proof of absence: a public-data day-ahead traffic report, a carbon signal (torus-cases-b.findings #29), plain-language plan explanations, quantified outcomes, compute as a flexible load, and what-if sizing for sales and IRP filings (torus-cases-b.findings #30).
- It never touches Torus's isolated station network (torus-cases-b.findings #13). It publishes a plan, and Lasso decides.

architecture:
One static web app, a small nightly data-prep job, and one optional serverless function. Nothing on the stage path needs the network.

1. prep/ (Python 3.13, standard library only)
- pandas and openpyxl are not installed on this PC, and they are not needed. The research scripts and my scratch parsers read OASIS zipped CSVs and the 75 MB PACE.xlsx with zipfile and xml.etree; the xlsx takes 14 s.
- fetch_oasis.py pulls:
  - PRC_LMP DAM for ELAP_PACE-APND, ELAP_PACW-APND, ELAP_PGE-APND and TH_SP15_GEN-APND (LMP plus the MCC congestion component);
  - SLD_FCST DAM (PACE load forecast);
  - the EDAM_WND_SLR_FORECAST_GRP GroupZip XML (PACE solar and wind);
  - PRC_INTVL_LMP RTM (5-minute prices for the live tile).
  Calls stay under 31 days, are spaced 5 s apart, and retry on HTTP 429.
- fetch_eia.py pulls the EIA-930 six-month BALANCE CSV filtered to PACE (demand and fuel mix) and parses PACE.xlsx into co2_hourly.csv.
- build_bundle.py joins everything on UTC interval start and writes public/data/bundle-YYYY-MM-DD.json. Each hour carries ts_utc, local_mt, lmp, mcc, load_fcst, solar_fcst, wind_fcst, net_load, co2_fcst, the other nodes' LMP, and provenance with a fetch timestamp.
- fit_carbon.py writes the regression coefficients, and backtest.py writes public/data/backtest.json.

2. engine/ (TypeScript, pure functions, vitest)
- score.ts, carbon.ts, plan.ts (the DP planner), crash.ts, fleet.ts (simulated archetype sites), campus.ts and explain.ts (plain-language templates).
- The same code runs in the browser and in tests, so on-stage re-planning is the tested code path.

3. app/ (Vite, React and TypeScript, SVG drawn with d3-scale and d3-shape; no map tiles)
- TrafficView: ribbon, sun arc, garage, shoulder lane and truck.
- RaceView: two lanes with meters.
- EngineerView: real curves, state-of-charge path, constraints and provenance.
- EventCard, BigNumbers with the assumptions drawer, and Controls: fleet slider from 1 to 500 MW, campus toggle, time-lapse, and CRASH on the space bar or clicker.
- LiveTile.

4. api/live.ts (optional single Vercel function)
- Fetches the OASIS RTM 5-minute PACE price on the server, because OASIS sends no CORS headers and returns zips. It caches for 5 minutes and falls back to the snapshot on any error or after 5 s.

5. Runtime
- Primary: `npm run preview` on the stage laptop with DATA_MODE=snapshot. A Vercel static deploy is the shareable copy and the QR target for judges' phones.

Data flow: on Tuesday at about 9:15-10pm MT, prep pulls Wednesday's day-ahead data, writes the bundle and commits it. The app loads the bundle, and the engine computes score, plan, race and numbers in the browser. Slider, crash and toggle actions re-run the engine locally. The live tile is the only runtime network call.

Precomputed: all market and EIA data, carbon regression coefficients, the May 1 to Oct 27 backtest, and Torus's 2025 call-hour distribution.
Live in the browser: the DP plan and re-plan (24 steps x 41 state-of-charge levels per site, a few ms), the crash response, fleet aggregation, the campus shift and the race meters.
Live over the network: only the RTM tile.

core_algorithms:
All of these are deterministic, explainable in one sentence, and sized for agents in hours.

1. Rush-hour score (traffic color), about 2 h
- For each hour of tomorrow, rank three things within the day: price, net load, and forecast CO2.
- score = 0.6 x price rank + 0.25 x net-load rank + 0.15 x CO2 rank.
- Colors: the top 4 hours are red (jam), scores under 0.35 are green (clear lane), the rest amber.
- explain.ts fills fixed templates: cheapest window, priciest window, biggest 2-hour solar drop, overnight-versus-midday price ratio.
- No LLM at runtime, so every sentence matches its number.

2. Carbon forecast for tomorrow, about 3 h including prep
- Fit by ordinary least squares on the last 90 days of EIA PACE hourly generated CO2, using EIA-930 actuals as features: CI = b0 + b1 x solar/load + b2 x wind/load + hour-of-day terms.
- Apply it to the EDAM solar and wind forecasts and the SLD load forecast.
- Report the error on the last 14 held-out days and show "forecast plus or minus MAE".
- Fallback: the hour-of-day mean of the last 30 days, labeled.

3. Fleet planner, dynamic programming over state of charge, about 5 h with tests
- Per site, 24 hourly steps (an optional 15-minute mode has 96).
- State: Pulse charge level on a 41-level grid, 0.05 MWh per MW for a 2 MWh/MW (0.5C) tank. Action: the next level.
- Reward: price x grid MW, minus a wear proxy ($10/MWh discharged), minus an optional carbon weight x CI x grid MW.
- Constraints:
  - charge no faster than min(P, host demand ceiling minus host load), so charging never sets a new 15-minute demand peak;
  - discharge no faster than P;
  - end charge equals start charge;
  - Spin held full at all hours and never used for arbitrage.
- Fleet: simulated archetype sites scaled to the slider MW.
- Proven in scratch Python: the Oct 27 plan charges 1-4pm and discharges 6-8pm for $57.54 per MW-day. With wear priced at $0 it would also cycle the morning ramp, so the wear proxy is what keeps it to one cycle a day.
- Wear: one cycle a day uses 365 of Pulse's 7,500 rated cycles a year, about 20 years.
- Acceptance test: within 1% of brute force on fixtures, and a re-plan under 50 ms in the browser.

4. Crash lane and event simulator, about 3 h
- The stage call fires at the judge's chosen minute.
- Spin ramps linearly to the site's call size (an assumption, 25% of station power) in 19 s, holds for 6 minutes, then recharges over 12 minutes from Pulse or the grid. The Spin page cites discharge and recharge in 12 minutes.
- The Pulse DP then re-solves from that minute using the updated charge level. The UI shows the plan change, its dollar cost and the re-plan time.
- Event-card metrics mirror Torus's published trace: ramp time against a 30 s target, delivered percentage against a 90-100% band.
- Year replay (Engineer view only): 359 calls drawn from Torus's 2025 hour histogram. All are answered by construction while Spin is reserved.
- Battery-only comparison: holding the same lane in Pulse costs about 3% of value in scratch (0.1 MWh/MW floor plus 25% headroom).
- No hour-pattern claims. The chart's time zone is unstated, and in my scratch run that alone swings the "calls a price-only plan would miss" figure from 14% to 77%.

5. AI campus, about 2 h
- A flat 100 MW baseline (simulated, sized like the first SB 132 contract of more than 100 MW).
- 25% can be deferred for up to 3 hours the same day: move it from the highest-score hours to the lowest, with Spin rate-limiting the step over about 6 minutes.
- Oct 27 in scratch: 75 MWh moved from 6-9pm to 1-4pm, $2,551 at day-ahead prices, about 16 t CO2 at EIA average intensity.

6. Backtest, about 2 h
- For every EDAM day from May 1 to Oct 27 (about 180 days), run three plans: habit (charge 1-5am, discharge in the same evening window), the timetable DP, and an unconstrained optimum.
- Score each in dollars and in CO2 at that day's actual EIA hourly intensity. Annualize as mean x 365 with a P10-P90 band.
- July and October in scratch: $14,500-17,700 per MW-year for the DP plan.

7. Race meters: pure playback of the two precomputed plans with running sums. No extra model.

risks: 'Lasso already does this.' Lasso claims ML forecasting, sub-250 ms dispatch and Spin/Pulse routing. Mitigation: pitch a nightly public-data plan that Lasso could ingest, never claim the split as new, say 'not advertised' and never 'Torus lacks', and ask what Lasso reads today.

The habit baseline could sound like a dig at Torus. Mitigation: it is the folk rule (night means off-peak), both lanes are Torus hardware, and the punchline is that Torus plus a better route earns 2.9x. Ask which signal sets charging today; it may be a rate schedule, and Utah's C&I tariff windows were not checked.

Average versus marginal emissions: the academic judge may push. Mitigation: label every CO2 figure as EIA average generated-basis intensity, show fossil share beside it, and note that the 'habit adds CO2' result holds even at 100% round trip. Marginal data for PACE (WattTime) is subscriber-only (prior-art.findings #26).

The time zone of Torus's 2025 heatmap is unstated. In scratch, how many calls a price-only plan would miss swings from 14% to 77% depending on the reading. Never claim an hour pattern; the judge picks the crash time, and the year replay shows readiness by construction only.

Wednesday's day-ahead may be dull, with a small spread. Mitigation: show it honestly ('light traffic tomorrow' is valid), keep Oct 27 and the May-Oct backtest as reference, and never silently swap in a better day.

Who captures the value. Dollars at EDAM prices are system value to Rocky Mountain Power's power costs, not Torus revenue, and a data center does not pay the EDAM price itself (utah-grid RISKS). Say 'value to the grid' and ask Torus how a fleet gets paid for daily peak management.

Simulated parameters are not Torus specs: Spin-to-Pulse ratio, call size, 88% round trip, $10/MWh wear. Company-reported figures (10C, 25,000 and 7,500 cycles, 500 MW, 99.9% uptime) are marketing claims; quote one source per number, and say 'up to 500 MW under MOU'.
The annualized $14,500-17,700 per MW-year rests on July and October only until the full backtest lands; winter and spring spreads may be smaller. Show a P10-P90 band from the full run.
Torus's data-center pages have returned 404 since Aug 2026 and 'AI' left its homepage headline (torus-intel.findings #12). Keep the AI campus as Act 2, about 20 seconds, not the spine.

Live data and venue failures: OASIS has no CORS, about one request per 5 s and occasional 429s, and venue Wi-Fi is unknown. Run snapshot mode locally, keep the live tile optional with a 5 s timeout, record a backup video by 3:30pm Wednesday, and carry a spare clicker (the space bar also works).
PACE is not Utah: it spans Utah, Wyoming and Idaho. Say 'PacifiCorp East' or 'Rocky Mountain Power's grid' when quoting the hourly mix, and do not call 10,173 MW a record.

Branding and likeness: no Torus logos or copied copy. Simulated sites are archetypes, never real customer names. Label stations 'Torus-style, simulated'. Do not imply any link to Torus's isolated station network.
Prior art: carbon-aware schedulers are the most common entry. The differentiation is storage physics (Spin and Pulse jobs), the crash lane and the Torus fleet, not 'greenest hour'.
Over-scope with an unknown team size. Hold the lane discipline, run cut checkpoints Tuesday at 1pm and 5pm, freeze features at 9pm Tuesday and code at 2pm Wednesday.
The show-of-hands opener can misfire if judges answer 'noon'. The line adapts: 'You're ahead of most people.'
